final_answer:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
RISK MEMORANDUM
To: Marcus Obi (GC); Diana Calloway. Re: Brightwell / Nordlicht Exclusive Distribution Agreement v4.2 (June 18, 2025). Perspective: Brightwell (Texas client). Assumes pre-signing posture (target July 15, 2025; comments due July 7). If later, the Effective Date, Contract Years and VitAlive dates are stale.

1. BOTTOM LINE
Do not sign v4.2 as drafted. Four deal-critical problems: (1) Brightwell's IP and compliance warranties are untrue on facts it already knows; (2) the draft contains EU-law hardcore and excluded restraints (resale price, post-term non-compete); (3) the CFO model assumes a launch the regulatory record says cannot happen; (4) Nordlicht's French investigation contradicts its Section 13.2 representation. A full-range launch on Sept 22-25, 2025 is unrealistic.

2. CRITICAL ISSUES

2.1 Trademark conflict (Sec. 12.1, 12.3, 15.3)
CPS found EUTM No. 018432156 "VITAEDGE" (Vitaedge Nutricion S.L.; Classes 5 and 29; registered Sept 8, 2022): identical mark, identical goods. Brightwell's U.S. registrations (5,891,204; 6,102,337) confer no EU rights. Use by Nordlicht would likely infringe EUTMR Art. 9(2)(a). Sections 12.1(b)-(d) warrant non-infringement and no known claims; Brightwell knows otherwise, so signing is a knowing false warranty. The 12.3 indemnity is outside the $5M cap and, because the carve-out opens 15.3, arguably outside the consequential-loss exclusion as well: rebranding, inventory, trade-show and sub-distributor losses are effectively uncapped. Knowing misstatement also supports fraud claims.
Options: acquire or license the mark; EU-specific rebrand; revocation for non-use (Art. 58(1)(a)) is unavailable until after Sept 8, 2027; invalidity for bad faith (Art. 59(1)(b)) only with evidence the filer knew of Brightwell's mark. An EUTM does not cover the UK, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland or Liechtenstein; CPS found no UK conflict but did not search Switzerland or EEA-EFTA registers, and Class 30 (bars) needs analysis.
Fix: delete or qualify 12.1 with a disclosure schedule; add a trademark-failure clause (suspension, reduced minimums, no-fault termination, capped rebranding contribution); cap 12.3 and exclude lost profits; disclose the facts (not the privileged memo) to Nordlicht, which may already know of the registration.

2.2 Regulatory readiness and compliance warranty (Sec. 4.1, 5.2, 11.2, 11.4)
Falkenberg (Apr 22) rates three SKUs HIGH: Neuro Focus and Collagen Renew (ashwagandha 600 mg; unsettled novel-food status; Denmark, France, Germany restrictions) and Iron Boost (65 mg iron versus about 25 mg guidance; Germany 6 mg, France 14 mg, Netherlands 45 mg). All 12 SKUs need relabeling; about 60% of claims must change or go; Immune+ (CO2 extraction) and Sleep Restore (melatonin) are medium. Novel-food authorization takes 18-24+ months; relabeling 8-12 weeks after claims sign-off, which Falkenberg said had to begin by early May. Nothing in the file shows it began, and the June model assumes no exclusions.
Section 11.4 has Brightwell warrant that all Products comply with all Territory law at shipment: false for at least three SKUs and, until relabeled, all twelve. Falkenberg expressly advised Brightwell not to give such a warranty. Breach feeds the 15.1(b) indemnity and, with knowledge, arguably "willful misconduct" outside the cap. Meanwhile 11.2 makes Nordlicht responsible for all approvals, notifications and claims, yet 4.1 gives Brightwell sole control and discretion over formulation and labeling, so Nordlicht cannot perform. No mechanism exists for excluded or delayed SKUs.
Fix: define "Cleared SKUs"; launch only those and add others by notice; limit 11.4 to conformity with specifications and law for cleared SKUs; allocate costs (reformulation and relabeling to Brightwell; national notifications to Nordlicht as importer and responsible food business operator under Reg. 178/2002); reduce minimums proportionately; add regulatory-change relief.
Reliability problems: (i) Falkenberg cites the novel-food regulation as "(EU) 2018/1015"; the correct instrument is Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 (as the draft cites), so its other citations need checking; (ii) it calls 25 mg an EFSA "tolerable upper intake level" while admitting EFSA set none; (iii) its ingredient lists differ from Exhibit A and the model: Sleep Restore melatonin 3 mg versus 5 mg in Exhibit A (a worse medicinal-classification risk), Protein+ whey versus pea/BCAA, Collagen Renew bovine versus marine, Immune+ echinacea, Neuro Focus Lion's Mane (Exhibit A and model; not assessed), Greens Blend probiotics (Exhibit A only). Re-run the assessment on actual specifications before anyone warrants anything. Member-state positions were not independently verified; local counsel should confirm. Novel-food status questions go to the first Member State of marketing under Art. 4 of Reg. 2015/2283.
Launch: displaying U.S. claims at Frankfurt invites enforcement (Reg. 1924/2006 reaches advertising and presentation).

2.3 EU competition law (Sec. 3.2, 6.2, 7.3, 9.1, 9.4, Exhibit C)
Regulation (EU) 2022/720 (VBER) is the safe harbor; Art. 101 TFEU applies because the agreement is implemented in the EEA, despite Texas law. UK and Swiss regimes run parallel and need separate advice.
- Resale price. Section 7.3 requires pricing within 10% of MSRP, recites "irreparable harm" and promises "corrective measures"; Exhibit C gives Brightwell final say. Wendt's Feb 5 email about coordinating "pricing and positioning across countries" worsens the optics. This reads as minimum or fixed pricing, a hardcore restriction (Art. 4(a)): the whole agreement loses the exemption, the clause is void (Art. 101(2)), and fines may reach 10% of worldwide turnover (Reg. 1/2003 Art. 23). Recommended prices are lawful only if genuinely non-binding. Delete the band, harm recital and corrective measures.
- Non-compete. Section 9.4's 18-month, Territory-wide post-term ban is outside the exemption (Art. 5(1)(b) tolerates only premises-limited, one-year, know-how protection) and likely unenforceable; it even survives Brightwell's own termination for convenience. In-term non-compete (9.1): a five-year term that auto-renews is tacitly renewable beyond five years, exempt only if the buyer can effectively renegotiate or terminate on reasonable notice; Nordlicht has no convenience termination right. "Competing Products" spans twelve categories and would capture Nordlicht's existing portfolio. Delete 9.4; cap or restructure 9.1; rely on confidentiality and trade-secret law.
- Sub-distributor flow-down ("no less restrictive") would push these restraints down the chain; limit it. Section 6.3 properly preserves passive sales. Confirm Brightwell's U.S. e-commerce does not ship into the Territory in breach of 2.2(a).

2.4 Nordlicht's French investigation (Sec. 13.2)
On May 20 Wendt disclosed that Nordlicht Distribution France SAS is in a dispute with French competition authorities over "distribution practices". Section 13.2 has each party represent that neither it nor any Affiliate is under governmental investigation. Nordlicht cannot give it truthfully, and Brightwell, knowing, cannot later claim reliance. A parent is presumed liable for a wholly controlled subsidiary (Akzo Nobel, C-97/08 P). If the conduct is price or territorial restriction, it bears directly on 7.3. Obtain the file and exposure assessment; add a disclosure schedule, specific indemnity, termination right and notification duty.

3. COMMERCIAL AND FINANCIAL RISKS

3.1 Minimums and model. Minimums total 1,370,000 units ($20,207,500 at $14.75); the model's arithmetic checks, but its premise (all 12 SKUs, no exclusions) is contradicted by Falkenberg. The three HIGH SKUs are 28,000 of 120,000 Year 1 units (23%). Without them the achievable base is about 92,000 units (77% of minimum): Nordlicht would need roughly 30% outperformance on remaining SKUs to avoid a Section 5.2 "material breach", and slippage crosses the 75% termination line (16.2). Brightwell would be pressing a shortfall it caused. Contract Year 1 also starts July 15 though launch cannot precede September, and there is no supply covenant (POs are rejectable). The model omits Nordlicht's EUR 340,000 cost-share request (EUR 170,000, about $183,600 at 1.08), which Castillo said on March 7 she was "open to discussing", and the draft is silent (18.4 would supersede it, but expect it to resurface); rebranding; relabeling and reformulation; any novel-food spend. Cost share alone cuts Year 1 net contribution from $503,800 to about $320,000. Its cross-references (Sec. 8.3, Exhibit B, Sec. 11.2) are wrong, some sensitivity figures do not reconcile to its formulas, and the 52% Nordlicht margin compares VAT-inclusive retail MSRP with Brightwell's transfer price, ignoring retailer margin, freight and duty, so real Nordlicht margin is far lower, raising shortfall and discounting pressure. A single transfer price across SKUs priced EUR 19.95-39.95 invites cherry-picking. Fix: re-base on cleared SKUs; ramp minimums; SKU-level mix; trademark and regulatory relief.

3.2 FX, credit. USD invoicing leaves FX risk with Nordlicht (a 10-20% EUR fall squeezes margin and raises shortfall risk); Net 60 is unsecured; 18% annual late interest should be checked against Texas usury limits.

3.3 Termination asymmetry. Brightwell may exit after 24 months on six months' notice without compensation; Nordlicht cannot. German courts may apply distributor goodwill-indemnity rules by analogy (section 89b HGB) and EU overriding mandatory rules may apply despite Texas law; sub-distributor terminations raise French (L.442-1 Code de commerce) and Belgian exposure. Flagged for local advice, not settled.

3.4 Sub-distribution (6.2). No consent or notice leaves Brightwell blind on regulatory capability, sanctions, recall traceability and trademark use; the trademark licence is non-sublicensable. Add notice, objection for cause, approved list, recall and audit cooperation, no sub-sub-distribution.

3.5 Patent gap. No European filings for BioEnhance; Brightwell's own U.S. publications defeat novelty (EPC Art. 54). CPS dated Paris priority from issue dates; it runs from first filing, though the conclusion holds. Exclusivity is purely contractual; the "foreign counterparts" language in the BioEnhance definition is empty. Strengthen trade-secret and no-reverse-engineering terms (Directive 2016/943), commission freedom-to-operate review, and do not market BioEnhance as patent-protected in Europe.

3.6 Liability and insurance. Only Nordlicht must carry product liability cover although Brightwell manufactures; confirm Brightwell's U.S. policy responds to EU sales and EU-forum suits. EU law treats an importer as producer (Directive (EU) 2024/2853 widens the regime); Iron Boost carries pediatric-poisoning exposure.

3.7 Data protection (Art. 14). Two sentences, no controller/processor roles or transfer mechanism (SCCs or EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework), and the transfer ban conflicts with recall and complaint cooperation. Add a short DPA.

3.8 Governing law and forum. Texas law and AAA/ICDR arbitration in Austin are workable (Nordlicht concedes). EU courts reviewing an award will apply Art. 101 as public policy (Eco Swiss, C-126/97); expect it as a defense to 7.3 and 9.4.

4. PRIVILEGE AND DISCLOSURE
Castillo's Apr 28 email called Falkenberg's findings "encouraging" with "a few areas" needing attention, understating three HIGH SKUs and a conclusion that the line cannot launch in its current form. Nordlicht's May 6 reply thanks her for the report "summary", so some disclosure occurred. Risks: privilege and work-product waiver; misrepresentation claims. Section 18.4's express non-reliance statement can bar fraudulent inducement under Texas law (Schlumberger v. Swanson, 959 S.W.2d 171 (Tex. 1997)), whereas a bare merger clause cannot (Italian Cowboy Partners v. Prudential, 341 S.W.3d 323 (Tex. 2011)); neither protects an express warranty in the contract, and German counsel may plead pre-contractual liability. Privilege is also thin: Castillo's Feb 10 email says she retained Falkenberg directly, while the report claims retention at counsel's direction in March. Stop sharing report content; send an accurate, factual written regulatory update.

5. DOCUMENT ERRORS TO FIX
Exhibit B says 31 countries but lists 32; Nordlicht operates in 18 countries yet gets exclusivity over all, with only "commercially reasonable efforts"; Section 8.1 is FCA but Castillo's email said "FOB Austin"; Nordlicht counsel's email is halbrechtvoss.de in the draft but halbrecht-voss.de in the correspondence; the last recital ends "; and" unfinished; the CPS memo cites the cap as 14.2 (it is 15.3), exclusivity as Section 5 (it is Art. 2) and minimums as Section 7 (it is 5.2), is dated May 1 yet cites the June 18 draft, and calls Dr. Castillo VP of R&D (she is CEO).

6. ACTIONS BEFORE JULY 7
1. Hold signature; phase the launch (cleared SKUs; UK first if the trademark persists).
2. Rewrite 12.1, 11.4 and 13.2 with disclosure schedules; add trademark and regulatory relief; cap 12.3.
3. Delete 7.3's band and 9.4; fix 9.1 and 3.2; obtain EU, UK and Swiss antitrust sign-off.
4. Diligence the French matter.
5. Re-run Falkenberg on actual specifications; reformulate or drop ashwagandha SKUs and Iron Boost; start the claims audit.
6. Rebuild the model.
7. Fix privilege handling; update Nordlicht in writing.
8. Instruct EU trademark counsel; add DPA and sub-distributor controls; confirm insurance.
Limits: EUR-Lex was blocked, so EU provisions were checked through secondary summaries; national-law points are flags for local counsel.
